v.rationale: All three pass their own suites (impl-1 20, impl-2 19, impl-3 29). I ran the same probe against each: no Accept header, expired and bogus tokens, the '*' ability, non-numeric ids, array references, a huge total, and 405s. Each one returns JSON with the right status and no class names (the custom 404 renderer hides the 'No query results for model [App\Models\Order]' message). The one behavioural difference was how middleware order interacts with route model binding. impl-3 binds {order} before the abilities check, so a token without orders:read gets 403 for another user's real order but 404 for an id that doesn't exist. That is an existence oracle, and it breaks the requirement to answer the same 404 as for an order that doesn't exist. impl-1 sees this coming and moves CheckAbilities ahead of SubstituteBindings, with a test for it. impl-2 avoids the problem by not using binding at all: it scopes findOrFail through the user's orders relationship. impl-1 ranks first for the most idiomatic combination (route ->can() plus a policy that returns denyAsNotFound) with no bugs. It loses points for the redundant redirectGuestsTo, a dead Order::saving line in a test, tests that mostly use actingAs instead of real tokens, and deleting the base example tests. impl-2 is just as correct and the simplest, and its tests use real tokens with debug off. It is a little less idiomatic (a string $order parameter, an unused 'ability' alias, and one vacuous 404/405 assertion). impl-3 has the best test suite and clean idioms, but the real requirement violation puts it last.
